newsitem.title: USA: U.S. says Israeli-Palestinian violence must stop.
newsitem.headline: U.S. says Israeli-Palestinian violence must stop.

text.p: The United States told Israel and the Palestinians on Friday that "the violence must stop" on the West Bank as Secretary of State Warren Christopher discussed the crisis with Israeli and Arab foreign ministers.

State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said U.S. officials were keeping up furious telephone diplomacy with the region as clashes in which more than 50 Palestinians and more than a dozen Israeli soldiers have died went into a third day.

Christopher, who has spoken twice with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Natanyahu by telephone but has not yet contacted Palestinian President Yasser Arafat, briefed President Bill Clinton, campaigning in Texas, on the situation.
"The United States is working very hard this morning, very intensively, to try to convince the Israelis and Palestinians to step back from the violence," Burns told reporters.

"Our message this morning to the populations in the West Bank, in Gaza, in Jerusalem and in Israel is that the violence must stop, that peace cannot be achieved in the street, it will not be won in the street," he said. "They have to turn their attention, turn their historical enmities and arguments and issues unresolved from the peace negotiations, back to the negotiating table."

Christopher, in New York for the U.N. General Assembly session, met first with Syrian Foreign Minister Farouq al-Shara and was later to meet Egyptian Foreign Minister Amr Moussa and Israeli Foreign Minister David Levy.

The meetings were scheduled before the eruption on Wednesday of the violence, sparked by an Israeli decision to open a tourist tunnel near an Islamic holy site in Jerusalem, but Burns said that subject would dominate the discussions.
He said the U.S. aim was to convince the Israelis and Arabs that a meeting must be arranged between Netanyahu and Arafat "or between their advisers."

White House spokesman Mike McCurry termed initial reports on the situation on Friday "encouraging," saying: "There does not seem to be any widespread violence, but today is Friday. As both communities move into their religious observances, we'll see what happens."

Former Secretary of State Lawrence Eagleburger said in a CNN television interview that Netanyahu appeared to have taken "a very hard line" in a news conference at which he called on Arafat to stop the "incitement."
Burns welcomed Israel's temporary closure for the Moslem and Jewish religious holidays of the controversial tunnel, saying he hoped it might "contribute to reducing the tensions that are so evident."
But diplomatic sources said Netanyahu had rebuffed an appeal by Christopher on Thursday to close the tunnel for a longer period, saying that would be giving in to violence.

"The image of the last three days is the image of decades past. It's the image of confrontation. But the reality of the last three or four years is that the Palestinians and Israelis have built something which can and should endure," Burns said.

He said Christopher had so far made no decision whether to travel to the region to try to salvage the Middle East peace process, which British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind said on Thursday could be "on the verge of collapse."

Burns said the United States would participate in a U.N. Security Council debate on the situation that was called by the Arab states on Friday but he made it clear Washington thought little good would come of it.

"I must say the focus of our efforts ought to be in the region. ... It's one thing to talk thousands of miles away from the events. It's quite more important, frankly, to try to use our influence where the violence is occurring," he said.
